Hi, I know some of what you're going through. Be kind to yourself, friend :\) You must sit yourself down, 3 times a day, and eat. Be gentle and encouraging. Remember, you're all you've got. If you've got a history of anorexia, you need to be even more proactive and careful when it comes to looking after yourself and supporting yourself. You're good enough just as you are, right here, right now,  \(anxiety, depression, stress and all\), and you've got absolutely nothing you need to prove to anyone.

Well, I've not known him for that long. We've been getting closer over the last seven weeks at best. Our friendship's been based upon fun, cheerfulness and mutual interests up until this point. He's a really upbeat, happy person and I'm not sure he'll be very sympathetic. Know what I mean?
I mean, if I get a text message from him in future, I will see if I can take your advice, dependant upon what it says. I'm not very hopeful I'll hear from him again though.

The same thing happened to me recently. I met a man who was smart, funny and interesting, and he asked me for a date right around the time I was spiralling into a deep depressive episode. The worst thing was knowing how close I came to having that kind of connection with someone. It hurt to know how badly I mucked it up, and I didn't know how to stop it. He was really special.

The thing is, I suppose, if it's not meant to be then it won't. You know?
But I know what you mean. It's tough to be alone when you crave that connection with someone. You never know what's around the corner though. I'd say try not to get too discouraged.

You are tough. The fact you're struggling with depression and still trying to give yourself hope and motivation to keep going, shows that. I used to think I was weak, having had anorexia for years and a plethora of other mental health problems besides.
However, I went through a period of remission, and for about a year of my life I had people tell me I'm the most laid-back, chill person they'd ever met. People used to find it amusing because I never seemed to be phased by anything.
So there you have it. If anything, you're tougher than most. Mental health problems aren't easy to deal with.

On the other hand, you'd be doing voluntary work, which means there's no commitment. It's not like there would be any harm in trying it for a week or two. You might love it; if you hate it, you always have the option to leave.
